The central question is: under what conditions do these learned biases interact with the sliding window boundary effects to create stable, self-reinforcing attention sinks — positions that act as probability mass dumps — and how does this pathology scale with context length? Key concepts include the attention sink phenomenon (first rigorously characterized in StreamingLLM), the distinction between structural sinks (induced by softmax normalization needing somewhere to dump probability mass when all keys are weak) and bias-amplified sinks (where learned positional terms actively steer logits toward fixed offsets), and the interplay between local receptive fields and the rare full-attention layers that can propagate sink structure globally. What a beginner misses is that the danger isn't just token positions being over-attended — it's that sink formation corrupts the residual stream at those positions, turning them into information bottlenecks that downstream layers read from heavily via value aggregation, meaning the sink tokens' value vectors get overwritten with a diffuse average of surrounding context rather than position-specific signal. The expert worry is specifically about the interaction between ALiBi-style slopes (which decay attention with distance, creating a recency-bias field) and the hard receptive field boundaries of sliding windows: at window edges, the slope gradient creates a sharp logit cliff that concentrates attention onto the nearest in-window tokens, and in hybrid architectures these boundary artifacts get periodically "laundered" through full-attention layers that then globalize the artifact.

The tightest bound on inference-time retrieval fidelity recovery is governed by what you can call the value subspace recoverability condition: if the sink token's value vector has already overwritten the residual stream at position i through weighted aggregation, no re-weighting of attention scores in the same layer can recover the original signal at i, because the value projection is a fixed linear map applied after softmax — meaning inference-time attention modification can only redirect future attention away from corrupted positions, not undo already-committed residual updates. Formally, if we define retrieval fidelity as the mutual information I(r; q) between a target token r and a query q at layer l, the maximum recoverable fidelity under inference-time intervention is bounded by I(r; q) ≤ I(r; V_l^clean) where V_l^clean is the value vector at r's position before sink contamination — and since V_l^clean is not accessible at inference time (the contamination is already baked into the residual stream by layer l), the practical bound depends entirely on how much of r's original signal survives in layers above l, which empirically approaches zero for sinks that form in layers 1–4 of a 32-layer model due to the residual stream's tendency to overwrite rather than additively preserve early-layer artifacts. The StreamingLLM inference patch (Xiao et al., 2023) implicitly acknowledges this bound by intervening at the attention mask level before sink formation rather than after — their "attention sink token" approach reserves position 0 as a designated sink absorber, which prevents diffuse contamination but does not recover fidelity for any context that was already processed through a sink-forming layer. Inference-time interventions that operate across layers — such as attention score modification at every layer simultaneously via a steering vector or activation patching — can in principle recover more, but the bound here depends on the rank of the contamination: if the sink-induced corruption is low-rank (a single dominant direction in the residual stream, as suggested by the mechanistic interpretability literature on attention patterns in GPT-2 and LLaMA), then a rank-1 or rank-2 inference-time correction via activation addition (as in Turner et al., 2023) can recover fidelity up to the noise floor introduced by all other attention heads that attended to the sink — empirically around 60–70% of baseline retrieval performance in needle-in-haystack tasks at 16k+ tokens.
